summary: This document defines DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement options that tell a host about encrypted DNS resolvers provided by its network. A host learns an authentication domain name, a list of IP addresses, and service parameters, for resolvers using DNS over HTTPS, DNS over TLS, or DNS over QUIC.

eli5.summary: When you join a network, it hands you a card listing its private phone lines for looking up names, along with their names and numbers.

questions: dhcp option for doh and dot
subtitle: DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement options that let a network tell hosts where its encrypted DNS resolvers are.

tldr.problem: Hosts joining a network normally learn only the IP address of its DNS resolver, which is not enough to set up DoH, DoT or DoQ with proper authentication.
tldr.mechanism: New DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Router Advertisement options carry an Authentication Domain Name, a list of IP addresses and service parameters encoded as SvcParams.
tldr.outcome: A host can connect to the network's encrypted resolver without extra lookups and authenticate it by name. The options are not themselves protected, so local spoofing must be mitigated separately.

today: RFC 9463 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. It works alongside RFC 9462, and its options take precedence over DDR when both are present.

sections.title: What DNR Does
sections.content:
RFC 9463 focuses on discovering encrypted DNS resolvers that use DNS over HTTPS (DoH), DNS over TLS (DoT) or DNS over QUIC (DoQ) in local networks. It does this with new DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) options. They convey the DNS Authentication Domain Name (ADN), a list of IP addresses and a set of service parameters. The procedure is called Discovery of Network-designated Resolvers (DNR).

Resolver selection and policies, including interaction with users, are out of scope, as is an inventory of the deployments the options can fit, for example local networks with or without DNS forwarders.
sections.eli5: A network can give your computer a card that says, "Here are our private, scrambled phone lines for looking up names."

sections.title: Design of the Configuration Data
sections.content:
The options always include an ADN, which the client uses as the reference identifier when it authenticates the resolver's certificate. This fits current practice, because certificates issued for IP addresses are a very small share of the total, according to the passage the RFC quotes from RFC 6125.

The options also return IP addresses so the host does not depend on another server to resolve the ADN. Each option ties a protocol to an address, so a client that supports more than one encrypted protocol does not need to probe. A list of addresses, ordered by preference, can support primary and backup resolvers. A single option carries both the ADN and the addresses so the two stay correlated when a network supports more than one ADN.

Service parameters follow the SvcParams wire format of RFC 9460. A DNR implementation MUST support alpn and port, and SHOULD support dohpath (RFC 9461). The parameters MUST NOT include ipv4hint or ipv6hint, because the included addresses supersede them.
sections.eli5: The card has the line's name, its phone numbers and its settings all in one place, so you never have to look anything up in a separate book.

sections.title: The Three Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option, OPTION_V6_DNR (code 144), holds a Service Priority, an ADN Length, the ADN, an Addr Length that MUST be a multiple of 16, the IPv6 addresses and the SvcParams. Addresses can be Link-Local, ULA or GUA. The DHCPv4 option, OPTION_V4_DNR (code 162), repeats a DNR Instance Data block for each resolver, with an Addr Length that MUST be a multiple of 4. If it exceeds the maximum DHCPv4 option size of 255 octets, the mechanism in RFC 3396 MUST be used.

The RA option (Neighbor Discovery type 144) adds a 32-bit Lifetime, the maximum time in seconds the ADN is valid. It SHOULD by default be at least 3 * MaxRtrAdvInterval, all one bits mean infinity, and zero means the ADN MUST no longer be used. The option is padded with zeros to a multiple of 8 octets.

If no port parameter is given, default ports apply: 853 for DoT, 443 for DoH and 853 for DoQ. In all three options, the address, SvcParams and their length fields are absent in ADN-only mode.
sections.eli5: The same card comes in three versions, one for each way a network can hand things out. They list the same things, and the router's version also says how long the card stays good.

sections.title: Client Behavior and Validation
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 client MUST include OPTION_V6_DNR in its Option Request Option, and a DHCPv4 client includes OPTION_V4_DNR in its Parameter Request List. Clients MUST be ready for several instances, each treated as a separate resolver and processed by service priority, where a smaller value means a higher preference. They MUST silently discard multicast and host loopback addresses.

On receipt, the client checks that the ADN is present and correctly encoded, and, if extra data is supplied, that the SvcParams are correctly encoded, that at least one valid IP address is present and that no ipv4hint or ipv6hint appears. If a check fails the option is discarded.

The client then uses ALPN identifiers to pick a protocol it supports and connects in priority order. It validates the resolver certificate with PKIX under RFC 5280, comparing the ADN to the certificate as described in RFC 6125, using the default system or application trust anchors unless configured otherwise.

An ADN-only mode is also possible, where the host gets only the ADN and sends SVCB queries itself. The RFC says the full mode SHOULD be used because it needs no additional DNS queries, and that ADN-only mode may be subject to active attacks, which DNSSEC can mitigate.
sections.eli5: Your computer reads each card, throws away broken ones, tries the best line first, and checks the line's name tag matches the name on the card before it talks.

sections.title: Conflicts and Other Networks
sections.content:
When resolvers are learned from both RA and DHCP, the rules in Section 5.3.1 of RFC 8106 MUST be followed. DHCP and RA options take precedence over Discovery of Designated Resolvers (RFC 9462), because DDR uses unencrypted DNS to an external resolver, which is open to both internal and external attacks.

If a client learns both unencrypted and encrypted resolvers from one network, and nothing is configured otherwise, it is RECOMMENDED to use the encrypted ones. It may fall back to the unencrypted resolver if it cannot establish an authenticated, encrypted connection.

Some networks, such as some cellular networks that use Protocol Configuration Options, cannot use these mechanisms. For other mechanisms, the RFC recommends providing at least a service priority where needed, a mandatory ADN, a list of IP addresses and a set of service parameters. Multihomed device resolver selection is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the network handed you a card, trust it over asking a stranger. If the private line will not connect, you may use the plain one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DHCP and RA messages are not encrypted or protected within the LAN, so an active attacker such as a compromised local device can spoof them and offer its own encrypted resolver, possibly one with a domain-validated public certificate. Mitigations include DHCPv6-Shield (RFC 7610), RA-Guard (RFC 7113) and SAVI for DHCP (RFC 7513). They help the endpoint get the configuration the server chose, but say nothing about who runs the server. A rogue resolver that spoofs an address will fail PKIX authentication against the ADN, but clients that ignore authentication failures are exposed.

If DHCP or RA messages are dropped, the client can fall back to a preconfigured encrypted resolver. A passive attacker can see that a host uses these options and so infer it can use DoH, DoT or DoQ, but cannot spoof or modify messages.

On wireless LANs, a shared pre-shared key lets an attacker mount an on-path attack, so the RFC advises unique credentials per client. Other than revealing support for the options, the RFC says it exposes no more privacy information than unencrypted DNS discovery options.
sections.eli5: Anyone on the local network could try to hand out a fake card. Checking the name tag on the line, and guards that block fake cards, keep you from calling a trickster.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA has assigned three codes. In the DHCPv6 Option Codes registry, OPTION_V6_DNR is 144, a Client ORO option that is not a singleton. In the BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options registry, OPTION_V4_DNR is tag 162. In the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Option Formats subregistry, the Encrypted DNS Option is type 144.
sections.eli5: Each version of the card gets its own official number so everyone recognises it.
